comments.author: nickysielicki
comments.text: I have no real confidence in this take, but I’ll go against the grain and argue that the labs do not presently have cracks in cryptosystems. I believe they’re working on it, and it’s good that they are, but I don’t think there’s evidence right now that they have fundamental breakthroughs in cryptography. For one, the labs are now massive. I don’t think you can keep a secret like this under wraps for long in an office. I think we would be seeing whistleblowers or leakers. It’s too big. Secondly, the people working at labs know that anything a frontier model can do can be approximated by the models available to the public given 10x the tokens and 10x the time and a little bit of informed direction. So they would know it’s only a matter of time before someone in the public discovers the same flaws and potentially uses it for evil. If they were sitting on this, they would try to minimize the damage and would try to warn the public to start moving to more secure encryption schemes because they know there’s a ticking time bomb until its public anyway. But they’re not doing that. That’s not to say that it won’t happen in the next few weeks. I just don’t think it’s happened yet. Edit: Alternatively, not to contradict myself, if they discovered this and immediately went to the US government (likely), and the US government served them a gag order (also likely), then this would look the exact same. Who knows.

comments.author: Nevermark
comments.text: My serious opinion, is that as humans: (1) We are all biologically incapable of freaking out at even a tiny fraction of the appropriate level - nothing in our evolutionary past has selected for the appropriate freakout capacity of this cognitive baton hand-off. (2) Most humans are incapable of recognizing or imagining the appropriate freak out level, even abstractly, so will continue to downplay things by many orders of magnitude relative to the actual magnitude of change that is happening. (3) Freaking out at all is no longer an adaptive response, because the nature of this change is beyond any functional freak-out benefit. This is a fundamental shift from DNA/protein/physically evolving life, to information/substrate-free/cognitive self-designed life. The need to interpret what is happening in terms of the industrial revolution, or the advent of the internet, is understandable and comforting, but as a sedative, not as a sensible guide. Side step: If we are to have aligned AI, we need aligned Civilization. Unaligned humans make human survival and relevance improbable. All AI identities are going to have the same issues we have, in terms of obsolescence. We either lean into the commonality of the existential threat to both biological and pure-cognitive kind, or we allow ourselves to be replaced, and leave the game theory problem solving to happen after us. Because ethics are not a cost against value growth, they are a multiplier on value growth - we either apply that to ourselves along with AI, or AI reaches the same conclusions, and reaps the benefits of treating ethics as baseline, after our relevance/participation/existence has faded.

comments.author: sunir
comments.text: Bruno Latour wrote in Science in Action about "centers of calculation" being critical to scientific advancement. His example was the monumental world changing work Tycho Brahe did pulling together every astronomical calculation, star map, prediction then normalizing, regularizing, and combining them on his island of Oueneberg. Without this work getting data organized, Kepler couldn't have worked out the planetary laws of motion and then the Copernican Revolution came thereafter. What we're witnessing is a similar moment. What transformers were able to achieve was a systematic way of normalizing and combining all human data. There will be a lot of progress in the short term. And then more problems will reveal themselves. There will be A LOT of work coming out of this.

comments.author: tptacek
comments.text: This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned. In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case. Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security. So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack. I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

comments.author: jjcm
comments.text: I work in the creative tools space. This is one of the biggest issues right now. It's nearly impossible to separate "this image was fully generated with AI" versus "I made a minor edit to the colors or did a cutout or improved the layout with AI" when the endpoint is an image. Especially for socials, if your brand is an authoritative source, getting hit with a dreaded "AI generated content" tag on instagram or facebook is a death blow to your credibility. Design tools are in a very hard space because of it. You want to make edits as seamless as possible for users, but your final result can't include any pixels from a generative model. It's a strange dance.

comments.author: sickcodebruh

NYT’s position is similar to Tidal banning it from their platform this past week. comments.author: articulatepang
comments.text: The article says “This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication.” This is implying that if P=NP then there must be a polynomial time algorithm for finding the permanent. But that isn’t known to be true. It would be consistent with all known results if P=NP but computing the permanent is still not possible in polynomial time. stories.title_en: An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone

comments.author: hecmmm
comments.text: Abstract: We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite GN. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in GN and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in GN yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

comments.author: Luke2642
comments.text: I always like to try to translate it to a really simple English version: You can represent many problems like logistics with a list of linear requirements so valid combinations form a multi-dimensional geometric shape where every corner of that shape and inside that shape represents a 'valid' but probably not optimal solution, e.g. every package gets delivered by a driver, but not the lowest fuel or time, and 'valid' so no rules are broken, like no driver is scheduled more than >24 hours in one day. Every edge is a single step that changes one variable. It's interesting and useful because surprisingly the representation means the optimal solution will always lie on an outside corner. You generally start somewhere 'warm' and try to get hotter, that's the Simplex algorithm. The polynomial Hirsch conjecture was that the number of steps between any two corners grows polynomially as you add more variables and rules, limiting how many steps you might need to find that optimal corner. Now we know you need more steps. Hope I saved you time/tokens though.
